result.markdown: --- title: "Session 1 — Missing Data: Patterns and Mechanisms" subtitle: "MCAR · MAR · MNAR · patterns · comparing complete and incomplete · testing · Lab 1" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - All earlier workshops quietly **dropped rows with missing values** - Today: **why that can mislead**, and how to **describe** missing data - By the end you can: - describe the **amount and pattern** of missingness - name the three **mechanisms** (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) - **explore** whether missingness depends on observed data - say what the data **cannot** tell you ::: ## Our data: an NCD cohort with gaps ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - **2,000 adults** (synthetic): age, sex, education, BMI, smoking, activity, SBP, HbA1c - Missing: **BMI 26%**, **HbA1c 21%**, **activity 12%**, **smoking 9%**, **SBP 6%** - Age, sex and education are complete - Only **45%** of adults have **every** variable ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ncd |> head(8) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 8 × 9 id age sex education bmi smoker activity sbp hba1c 1 C0001 50 Female Secondary+ 26.4 0 3.2 117 5.2 2 C0002 63 Male Secondary+ NA 1 0.8 164 NA 3 C0003 64 Female Primary 23.7 0 3.8 118 NA 4 C0004 62 Female Secondary+ NA 0 4.7 128 5.8 5 C0005 73 Male Secondary+ 22.2 1 4.3 130 5.2 6 C0006 26 Male None 21.7 0 7.7 118 5.4 7 C0007 62 Female None 34.8 0 1.4 143 NA 8 C0008 45 Female Secondary+ 26.3 0 7.8 132 5.1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: # Topic 1 — Mechanisms {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Three mechanisms | Mechanism | Missingness depends on... | Example here | |---|---|---| | **MCAR** (completely at random) | nothing | a form lost at random (smoking, 9%) | | **MAR** (at random) | **observed** data | BMI missing more in **older men with a high SBP** | | **MNAR** (not at random) | the **missing value itself** | high **HbA1c** more often missing | ::: {.key} The names are confusing: in **MAR** the missingness is **not random** at all; it is **explained by other observed variables**. That is what allows us to **correct** for it. ::: ## Why it matters ::: {.incremental} - **MCAR**: complete-case analysis is **unbiased** but loses **precision** - **MAR**: complete-case can be **biased**; **multiple imputation** (and likelihood methods) are **valid** - **MNAR**: **no method** is valid without an **assumption** about the missing values: do a **sensitivity analysis** - You **cannot tell MAR from MNAR** from the observed data alone ::: # Topic 2 — Describing missing data {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## How much and which pattern? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(100 * colMeans(is.na(ncd)), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` id age sex education bmi smoker activity sbp 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.0 26.4 9.2 12.2 5.9 hba1c 20.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(complete.cases(ncd)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 905 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} md.pattern(dat, plot = FALSE) |> head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` age sex education sbp smoker activity hba1c bmi 905 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 296 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 1 196 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} **905** adults (45%) are complete; then **BMI alone missing (296)** and **HbA1c alone (196)**: **26 patterns** in all. ::: ## A picture ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} gg_miss_upset(dat, nsets = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_patterns_mechanisms_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.key} An **UpSet plot** shows the commonest **combinations** of missing variables. Also useful: `vis_miss(dat)` and `miss_var_summary(dat)`. ::: # Topic 3 — What drives the missingness? {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Compare with and without BMI ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> group_by(bmi_missing = is.na(bmi)) |> summarise(n = n(), age = round(mean(age), 1), sbp = round(mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE)), men = round(mean(sex == "Male"), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 bmi_missing n age sbp men 1 FALSE 1472 45.3 121 0.44 2 TRUE 528 53.9 135 0.63 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} Adults with a missing BMI are **older (54 vs 45)**, **more often men (63% vs 44%)** and have a **higher SBP (135 vs 121)**. The data are **not MCAR**. Because the differences are in **observed** variables, **MAR** is plausible. ::: ## Model the missingness ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_miss <- glm(is.na(bmi) ~ age + sex + education + sbp, data = dat, family = binomial) round(summary(m_miss)$coefficients, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) -16.339 0.855 -19.107 0.000 age 0.025 0.005 4.637 0.000 sexMale 0.729 0.126 5.765 0.000 educationPrimary 0.165 0.157 1.053 0.292 educationSecondary+ 0.082 0.155 0.530 0.596 sbp 0.106 0.007 16.131 0.000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Age, male sex and **especially SBP** (z = 16) predict a missing BMI; education does not - This is evidence for **MAR**: and a warning that **SBP, the outcome, must be in the imputation model** ::: ## Little's MCAR test ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> mutate(male = as.integer(sex == "Male")) |> select(age, male, bmi, smoker, activity, sbp, hba1c) |> mcar_test() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 statistic df p.value missing.patterns 1 772. 118 0 26 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} p < 0.001: **MCAR is rejected**. That does **not** prove **MAR**: **MNAR cannot be tested** from the data, because the values that decide it are the ones **you do not have**. Argue it from **subject knowledge** (why would a value be missing?), then do a **sensitivity analysis** (Session 5). ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 1 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `missing-workshop/labs/lab1_pattern.R` - percent missing, complete cases, patterns - UpSet plot and a table of missingness - who is missing: comparison, logistic model, Little's test ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m1q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="hjwt0o.mn47uq" data-show="TWlzc2luZyBhdCByYW5kb206IG1pc3NpbmduZXNzIGRlcGVuZHMgb24gb2JzZXJ2ZWQgdmFy aWFibGVz" data-explain="TWlzc2luZ25lc3MgdGhhdCBpcyBleHBsYWluZWQgYnkgb2JzZXJ2ZWQgYWdlLCBzZXggYW5k IFNCUCBpcyB0aGUgZGVmaW5pdGlvbiBvZiBNQVIuIE1OQVIgY2Fubm90IGJlIHJ1bGVkIG91 dCBmcm9tIHRoZSBkYXRhLCBidXQgTUFSIGlzIHRoZSB3b3JraW5nIGFzc3VtcHRpb24gaGVy ZS4="} Older men are more often missing BMI, and they also have a higher observed SBP. Which mechanism is the most plausible? - Missing at random: missingness depends on observed variables - Missing completely at random: missingness is unrelated to the data - Missing not at random: missingness depends on the unobserved BMI itself - No mechanism applies, since a part of the BMI values is observed ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m1q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="hjx69e.mn4mc4" data-show="VGhlIGRhdGEgYXJlIG5vdCBNQ0FSLCBidXQgdGhpcyBkb2VzIG5vdCB0ZWxsIE1BUiBmcm9t IE1OQVI=" data-explain="UmVqZWN0aW5nIE1DQVIgc2hvd3MgdGhhdCBtaXNzaW5nbmVzcyBkZXBlbmRzIG9uIHNvbWV0 aGluZy4gV2hldGhlciB0aGF0IGlzIG9ic2VydmVkIChNQVIpIG9yIHVub2JzZXJ2ZWQgKE1O QVIpIGNhbm5vdCBiZSBsZWFybmVkIGZyb20gdGhlIHRlc3Qu"} Little's test rejects MCAR (p < 0.001). What can you conclude? - The data are MNAR, so multiple imputation cannot be used on them - The data are not MCAR, but this does not tell MAR from MNAR - The data are MAR, since MCAR is the other simple mechanism left - Nothing can be concluded, because the test applies to categorical variables ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m1q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="hjxji5.mn50tj" data-show="VGhlIHZhbHVlcyB0aGF0IGRldGVybWluZSB0aGUgbWlzc2luZ25lc3MgYXJlIG5vdCBvYnNl cnZlZA==" data-explain="TU5BUiBtZWFucyBtaXNzaW5nbmVzcyBkZXBlbmRzIG9uIHRoZSBtaXNzaW5nIHZhbHVlIGl0 c2VsZi4gV2l0aG91dCB0aG9zZSB2YWx1ZXMgdGhlcmUgaXMgbm90aGluZyB0byBjb21wYXJl LCBzbyB0aGUgYXNzdW1wdGlvbiByZXN0cyBvbiBzdWJqZWN0IGtub3dsZWRnZSBhbmQgc2Vu c2l0aXZpdHkgYW5hbHlzaXMu"} Why can MNAR not be tested using the observed data? - The sample is too small for a test to be able to detect the effect - Tests exist for it, but they need survey weights in order to work - MNAR occurs when a large share of the values (above half) is missing - The values that determine the missingness are not observed ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m1q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="hjxwqr.mn5fat" data-show="SXQgbG9zZXMgcHJlY2lzaW9uLCBhbmQgbWF5IGJlIGJpYXNlZCBpZiBjb21wbGV0ZSBjYXNl cyBhcmUgc2VsZWN0ZWQ=" data-explain="TW9yZSB0aGFuIGhhbGYgb2YgdGhlIHNhbXBsZSBpcyBkaXNjYXJkZWQsIGFuZCBpZiBtaXNz aW5nbmVzcyBkZXBlbmRzIG9uIHRoZSB2YXJpYWJsZXMgaW4gdGhlIGFuYWx5c2lzLCB0aGUg cmVtYWluaW5nIGFkdWx0cyBhcmUgYSBzZWxlY3RlZCBncm91cC4="} Only 45% of adults are complete. What is the main problem with complete-case analysis here? - It loses precision, and may be biased if complete cases are selected - It makes the standard errors too small, because fewer adults are analysed in the model - It turns the variables into categories, which loses information on each variable - It cannot be run in R unless the missing values are first recoded as zero ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m1q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="hjy9zi.mn5ts8" data-show="V2hpY2ggdmFyaWFibGVzIGFyZSBtaXNzaW5nIHRvZ2V0aGVyLCBhbmQgd2hlcmUgaW1wdXRh dGlvbiBtYXR0ZXJzIG1vc3Q=" data-explain="QSBwYXR0ZXJuIHRhYmxlIGRlc2NyaWJlcyB0aGUgYW1vdW50IGFuZCBjb21iaW5hdGlvbnMg b2YgbWlzc2luZ25lc3MuIEl0IGRvZXMgbm90IGlkZW50aWZ5IHRoZSBtZWNoYW5pc20gb3Ig dGhlIG51bWJlciBvZiBpbXB1dGF0aW9ucy4="} A pattern table shows 905 complete rows and 296 rows with only BMI missing. What does it help you decide? - Whether the missing values in this dataset are random or not random in nature - Which adults should be deleted from the dataset before the analysis starts - Which variables are missing together, and where imputation matters most - How many imputations are needed to get unbiased estimates from the data ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **MCAR / MAR / MNAR**: what the missingness depends on - **Describe**: % missing, complete cases, patterns, plots - **Compare** observed variables between complete and incomplete; model the missingness - **MNAR cannot be tested**: argue it, then do a sensitivity analysis - Include the **outcome** among the variables that explain missingness ::: **Next:** Session 2: simple methods and why they fail

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
